title: Kibbeh nayyeh
subtitle: Lebanese raw bulgur and lamb tartare
excerpt: Kibbeh nayyeh is a Lebanese dish of raw lamb mince worked together with fine bulgur, onion, and spices into a smooth, fresh-tasting paste. It is eaten immediately, spread on a plate and dressed with olive oil, raw onion, and mint. Only use the freshest lamb from a trusted butcher.
sourceNotes: Claudia Roden, A Book of Middle Eastern Food (1968). Kibbeh nayyeh documented as a traditional Levantine raw meat preparation. Anissa Helou, Lebanese Cuisine (1994). Sourcing requirements, spice blend, and the cultural context of raw meat eating in Lebanon described in detail.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Kibbeh nayyeh must be prepared and eaten immediately. Do not store raw.

content.text: Kibbeh nayyeh is a Lebanese raw lamb and bulgur preparation, similar in concept to beef tartare but with a grain base and a distinct spice blend of allspice and cinnamon. The lamb and bulgur are processed together until smooth and the mixture is served immediately at room temperature, dressed with olive oil and mint. Sourcing is critical: use only freshly ground lamb from a butcher you trust, ideally ground the same day. Do not prepare this dish with supermarket pre-packed mince.

attrs.text: Only use freshly ground lamb from a trusted butcher, ground the same day. This is not a dish for pre-packed supermarket mince.

items.prepNote: very fresh, finely minced by your butcher on the day
fine bulgur, rinsed and soaked in cold water for 20 minutes, then squeezed dry

content.text: Soak {{bulgur-wheat}} in cold water for 20 minutes. Drain and squeeze very firmly in a clean cloth until as dry as possible.

Place the fresh {{lamb-leg}} mince in a food processor with the squeezed bulgur, grated {{onion}}, {{allspice}}, {{cinnamon-ground}}, {{black-pepper}}, and {{sea-salt-fine}}. Process for one to two minutes until the mixture becomes very smooth and almost paste-like.
Taste for seasoning and adjust if needed. Spread the mixture on a large plate or in a shallow dish, pressing it flat and making shallow grooves with the back of a spoon.
Drizzle {{extra-virgin-olive-oil}} over generously. Scatter {{mint}} leaves and sliced {{onion}} over the top. Serve immediately with warm {{pitta-bread}}.

items.symptom: The mixture is sticky and hard to spread
items.fix: Squeeze harder. The bulgur must be as dry as possible or it makes the mixture wet and difficult to work.

items.symptom: The texture is grainy rather than smooth
items.cause: Fine bulgur not soaked long enough, or coarser bulgur used
items.fix: Soak for at least 20 minutes. Use the finest grind available (number 1). Coarser bulgur will not become smooth even after processing.

items.symptom: The lamb smells off or sour
items.fix: Do not use this meat for kibbeh nayyeh. Fresh lamb should smell clean and sweet. Discard and source from a reliable butcher.
Ground spices lose potency and can taste bitter with age. Use freshly bought spices and measure carefully.

content.text: Kibbeh nayyeh is one of the most important dishes in Lebanon, eaten at celebrations and family gatherings and treated with care. Lebanese home cooks take pride in it; the freshness of the lamb is not negotiable. It is linked to mountain villages in Lebanon and to Christian communities who eat it on certain feast days. Guests who eat it with enthusiasm show they know Lebanese food. Raw meat dishes exist in many cultures from beef tartare to carne cruda, but kibbeh nayyeh stands apart for its grain base and Levantine spice profile.
